body.heading: The oldest clock there is
paragraphs: Long before watches and phones, people told the time by a shadow. A sundial is just a flat plate with a raised edge — called a gnomon — that casts a shadow as the Sun moves across the sky. As the day passes, the shadow sweeps around the plate like the hand of a clock.

Sundials have been used for thousands of years, in Egypt, Greece, Rome and China. They only work in sunshine, and they tell solar time, which can differ a little from clock time — but on a sunny afternoon, your own sundial will be close enough to tell you when lunch is over.

body.heading: Build and watch it work
paragraphs: You need a sunny spot and a flat surface. Draw a circle on a paper plate and mark twelve lines around it like a clock face, then push a pencil upright through the centre so it stands like a little tower. Point the top of the pencil roughly toward the north — a compass app can help — and tilt it slightly, the way the Earth's axis tilts.

Then watch. The pencil's shadow will fall on one of your lines, and over an hour it will move to the next. Mark where the shadow lands every half hour and write the time beside it. By the end of the afternoon you will have a clock that runs on nothing but sunlight — and a good sense of how the Sun walks across the sky.

description: With a paper plate, a pencil and a sunny afternoon, build the oldest clock there is — and watch the Sun do the telling.

safetyNotes: Do this activity in daylight with sun protection on — hat, sunscreen and water on a hot day.
